newsitem.title: FRANCE: LVMH rallies on Arnault comeback.
newsitem.headline: LVMH rallies on Arnault comeback.

text.p: Shares in LVMH rallied to an all time high on Thursday after British groups Guinness and Grand Metropolitan agreed to consider LVMH chairman Bernard Arnault's alternative proposal to their planned merger.

"By putting pressure on the legal front and through the stock market, Arnault has managed to turn the situation around. He's obliged the British companies to look at his plan. The market is applauding his success," a broker said.
LVMH's stock finished up 3.67 percent at 1,638 francs after having touched an all time high of 1,660 francs and outperformed the Paris bourse's CAC-40 index, which closed up 0.95 percent.
"Arnault has scored a point but it's premature to talk of victory," another broker said.

Arnault said his proposal for an independent, listed company grouping LVMH's Moet Hennessy wine and spirits businesses with the drinks activities of Guinness and GrandMet would create more value for the shareholders of the three companies than the planned Guinness-GrandMet merger plan announced in May.
Share analysts say Arnault must now prove that his proposal will create more shareholder value all-round.
Several analysts were not convinced that GrandMet and Guinness shareholders would come out winners, but Arnault's plan has its backers.

"I think it would create more value," said John Wakely at Lehman Brothers. He estimated the difference at "at least a couple of billion sterling" or 10 to 15 percent more than the value generated by the 24 billion pound ($40.2 billion) Guinness-GrandMet deal.

Guinness's brewing and GrandMet's food businesses would be worth more independently, he said. Although those businesses have outperformed the spirits activities, that is not fully reflected in the share prices of Guinness and GrandMet because the groups are valued as distilled spirits companies.

Analysts say LVMH would hold 30 to 35 percent of the drinks group with a portfolio of brands including Moet & Chandon and Pommery champagnes, Hennessy cognacs, Guinness's Johnny Walker and Dewar's whiskies and GrandMet's Smirnoff, J&B and Baileys.

Arnault has a good record in terms of creating shareholder value. Between 1992 and 1996, LVMH's stock has been among the biggest gainers of the Paris bourse's blue-chip CAC-40 issues. In the past 12 months, it has risen 30 percent.
But its performance has lagged some of the other blue-chips and taken a few knocks since the company began buying GrandMet stock in mid-June to force the British companies to negotiate.
"They had tried to exclude their largest shareholder from Day One. That's silly," one analyst said.
LVMH has spent more than 8 billion francs ($1.4 billion) since mid-June to buy 6.4 percent of GrandMet in an apparent bid to line up votes to block the planned merger.

LVMH previously took legal action against Guinness -- in which it holds 14.2 percent -- to defend its right to buy Guinness out of their valuable distribution ventures, which hold the rights to market Guinness brands in France, the United States and much of the Far East for 10 years.

Analysts say Arnault is fighting to keep from being marginalised in the drinks business by the Guinness-GrandMet megamerger and having his capital locked up in a subsidiary of the new drinks-to-fast-food GMG Brands.
"For LVMH, a three-way deal is indispensable," a Paris analyst said.

Arnault has said he is committed to the drinks business. While less profitable than luxury goods, drinks are less exposed to the vagaries of fashion, he says. ($ = 0.596 British Pounds) ($ = 5.907 French Francs)
